extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians and performers (especially those using props); comedy writers and act developers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and evaluating prop-based stand-up comedy routines, describing structural mechanics, common techniques, performer-specific approaches (Carrot Top vs Gallagher), and an explicit evaluation rubric for props and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup with prop
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an ordinary arrangement so the audience recognizes normal function and context; this establishes the baseline that can later be subverted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster expectation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally create an expectation of how the prop will be used; clear, familiar cues help make the later reveal or twist more impactful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subvert via reveal
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden new function, malfunction, unexpected use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The payoff comes from revealing an unexpected use or failure of the prop; timing and clarity of the reveal are critical so the audience immediately understands the twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdirection
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange visual or verbal cues to lead the audience toward one interpretation, then flip it; misdirection supports both surprise and laugh timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the prop enable the joke (not just decorate)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the prop enable the joke (not just decorate)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the prop is integral to the punchline — if the object only decorates the stage, it may dilute rather than strengthen the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is there visual/verbal interplay?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good prop comedy uses both channels: the object and the spoken line should interact so the combined effect is funnier than either alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the prop quickly readable by the audience?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the prop quickly readable by the audience?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Props must communicate at a glance (shape, size, obvious function) so audience members can register the setup and be primed for the punch; avoid overly complex or ambiguous props unless the ambiguity is the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the routine maintain energy through transitions?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the routine maintain energy through transitions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitions between props/jokes should be fast and keep momentum; Carrot Top-style quick resets are one model, whereas spectacle acts may accept slower, theatrical transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could the joke work without the prop? If yes, why use it?
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the joke work without the prop? If yes, why use it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the joke stands alone verbally, question whether the prop adds value (visual reinforcement, surprise, spectacle) or is redundant; use props when they amplify or change the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carrot Top's approach: compact one-liners and quick resets
rubrics_metrics.description: Dozens of props in trunks on stage. Each joke: pull out prop, deliver one-liner describing it, toss away. Compact, pun-based contraptions. Cleaner setups, quicker resets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design props that read instantly and support a succinct verbal tag; prioritize speed, economy, and a steady rhythm of visual gag → one-liner → clear reset. Influences include Steve Martin (absurdity), Gallagher (visual gags), Tonight Show (clean structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gallagher's approach: spectacle-driven signature set-piece
rubrics_metrics.description: Sledge-O-Matic: smashing watermelons on stage. Audience showered in debris. Wild, messy, theatrical. One signature prop / set-piece dominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model emphasizes a large theatrical payoff and audience spectacle over rapid-fire turnover; craft a central visual moment that justifies its mess and runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual pun
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual pun: object embodies a wordplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create props that literally or visually represent a verbal double-meaning so the sight-line and the language double up the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical malfunction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design controlled failure or 'malfunction' moments that appear accidental but are staged for comedic effect; ensure safety and repeatability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repurposing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a familiar object and give it an unexpected function; clarity in the original function helps make the misuse funnier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurd specificity: prop is too specific to be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerate detail to absurd levels (an object that solves an impossibly niche problem) to highlight the silliness; specificity can increase the surreal humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition with variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition with variation: each prop similar form, different punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a recurring format or motif across multiple props but vary the punchline each time to build expectation and then subvert it for laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why props work: visual + verbal channel
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual + verbal channel: doubled punch. Object = something concrete the punch can attach to. Breaks the 'one comedian, one mic' monotony. Creates spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the combined impact of sight and sound: props give comedians a concrete target for jokes, diversify stage dynamics, and can create moments of spectacle that pure stand-up may not.
